Description: The guidance requires public companies to disclose material business risks to investors, transparently through regular filings with the SEC, including climate change risks that may develop on their business.
The regulation requires listed companies to “adopt and disclose a code of business conduct and ethics.”
The regulation clarifies that ESG factors can be a part of the primary analysis of cautious investment decision making.
The Consultation contains policy proposals to modernize Ontario’s capital markets for enhancing ESG disclosure including forward-looking information, for Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) issuers.

The regulation states that any “material” information on the environment or social aspects must be immediately disclosed by a news release as required by the Exchanges’ Timely Disclosure Policies. The issuer must file a material change report on the System for Electronic Document Analysis and Retrieval (SEDAR).
Under this regulation mining companies are required to report on reasonably available information on environmental and social factors as it involves various mining and exploration activities.
SFDR is designed to obligate financial market participants (FMPs) and financial advisers to be transparent with their sustainable investment products and to prevent greenwashing.

Regulation: EU Taxonomy Regulation Article 8 Delegated Act
Description: The EU Taxonomy framework is designed to categorize economic activities to help fund managers, companies, issuers and project promoters navigate the transition to a low-carbon, climate-resilient, and resource-efficient economy. The taxonomy will increase transparency and facilitate green bonds in sustainable projects and assets across the EU.

The initiative was established to improve the EU regulatory framework on company law and governance by helping companies manage long-term sustainability goals such as social and human rights, climate change, environmental protection, etc. by introducing a duty of care and mandatory due diligence.
It requires public companies with more than 500 employees to provide accurate data on social and environmental practices they have adopted to aid shareholders.

Regulation: German Supply Chain Due Diligence Legislation
Description: The act will go into effect on January 1, 2023, requiring the applicable companies to determine and assess risks to human rights and the environment within their supply chains, as well as to establish effective risk management systems. The act is applicable to German-based companies having more than 3,000 employees, and the threshold will be reduced to 1,000 starting January 1, 2024.
The Klimaatakkoord contains agreements with specific sectors to achieve climate goals. The listed sectors are: electricity, industry, built environment, traffic and transport, and agriculture.
The regulation requires commercial companies with a premium listing to disclose in line with the TCFD recommendations.

Regulation: Mandatory Climate-related Financial Disclosures by Publicly Quoted Companies, Large Private Companies and LLPs (Non-binding guidance)
Institution: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
Description: The guidance helps companies and limited liability partnerships (LLPs) understand how to meet new mandatory climate-related financial disclosure requirements.

Regulation: Articles 964a-964c of the Code of Obligations
Description: Swiss companies of public interest must prepare an annual report on non-financial matters covering environmental issues, social issues, employee-related issues, human rights, and combating corruption.

Regulation: Article 964j-964l of the Code of Obligations
Description: Registered companies in Switzerland must comply with obligations of due diligence in the supply chain and report if: 1. they place in free circulation or process in Switzerland minerals containing tin, tantalum, tungsten or gold or metals from conflict-affected and high-risk areas; or 2. they supply products or services that are produced by child labor.

Regulation: Environmental Risk Management for Asset Managers, Banks and Insurers
Description: The guidance lays out expectations for asset managers, banks, and insurers to improve the resilience of funds and segregated mandates they manage by laying out effective environmental risk management procedures that can be implemented.
Proposed in 2015, the regulation went through changes in 2020 for introducing ESG mandatory requirements for corporations. There is a requirement to report on the environmental and social factors.

Regulation: Circular to Management Companies of SFC-authorized Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds – ESG Funds
Institution: Securities and Futures Commission of Hong Kong
Description: By enhancing the disclosure standard of ESG funds, the circular aims to improve their comparability, transparency and visibility.

Items 7 and 10 of Annex 24 require listed corporations to include the following environmental sustainability information in their yearly reports: environmental policies, costs for compliance with environmental regulations and international standards, and third-party assurance check.

Institution:
Companhia de Tecnologia de Saneamento Ambiental de Brasil

(CETESB)
Description: CETESB in São Paulo requires companies in highly polluting industries such as manufacturing and energy to report scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions.

This resolution sets out guidelines for listed entities to “carry out their activities with good faith, loyalty and diligence” and “ensure high ethical standards” in the application of resources. Article 10(4) states these entities “should consider in the analysis of risks, whenever possible, the aspects related to economic, environmental, social and investment governance sustainability”.
The code outlines core principles for successful corporate governance with the goal of achieving mid to long-term growth and increasing corporate value.

Regulation: ESG-related Amendments to the Disclosure Rules Applicable to Listed Companies
Description: The act mandates that companies, corporations and investors report on disclosure principles, content, and scopes, as well as liabilities, emphasizing the necessity of transparency for both companies and investors.

Regulation: Measures for the Assessment of Information Disclosure of Listed Companies on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (2020 revision)
Description: These metrics analyze whether listed firms have taken the initiative to disclose their ESG performance, as well as if the substance of their disclosure reports is comprehensive and complete enough to assess their social responsibility.

Institution: Australian Government, Workplace Gender Equality Agency
Description: This act requires non-public sector companies with more than 100 employees to submit a report to the Workplace Gender Equality agency annually, detailing the gender composition of their workforce, the gender composition of their governing bodies, gender remuneration, and anything else related to gender-based harassment and discrimination.

Regulation: ASX Corporate Governance Principles and Recommendations: 4th edition
Description: By focusing on material environmental and social risks, the fourth edition of the law pushes listed firms to strengthen climate and non-financial risk disclosure.

Regulation: National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Regulation (NGER)
Institution: Australian Government, Department of the Environment and Energy
Description: NGER was developed as a framework for energy and emissions reporting. The Determination 2008 provides methods for calculating GHG emissions and energy data provided by the NGER act. Amendments to this act are made annually.

Companies filing director’s reports must disclose social and environmental information, as well as ethical information, under this Act. It also applies to superannuation funds, which must explain how environmental, social, and governance factors are factored into investment decisions.
